verdicts.reason: Both score the presence of a concrete implementable alternative plus an explanation of how it still serves the proposal's stated objective, with identical zero anchors.
Identical list of monitoring elements (indicators, data collection, verification, reporting, revisit triggers) and the same zero anchor; only the framing sentence order differs.
Both ask whether a concrete alternative regulatory design is specified at implementable granularity; 'proposes nothing' and 'only objects' pick out the same low end.
Word-for-word the same construct: whether the whole argument rests on first-person anecdote with no external citation, data, or source.
Same enumerated workflow markers (forms, offices, transition steps, testing scenarios, timelines, documentation) and the same 'general preference only' floor.
Both score whether the text claims to speak for multiple named organizations, a membership, or a consensus process versus an individual submission.
Both score explicit disclosure of prior permits, recurring meetings, ongoing communications, or past dealings with the agency; the added 'presence not authority' note only sharpens it.
Both score whether a reasoned failure mechanism is spelled out for why the rule would not produce the intended effect, judging reasoning rather than tone.
Both score whether new information (measurements, operational records, surveys, field observations) with a stated source enters the record, versus opinion only.

Both score commenter-derived numeric compliance-cost estimates with the basis stated; the renaming from 'dollar estimates of burden' to 'quantifies cost using own data' does not shift the property scored.
Both score accurate connection of the proposal to statutory language, delegated authority, precedent, or legal limits, with unsupported legal assertions at zero.
Both require concrete firsthand observation carried up to a rule-relevant generalizable pattern, with bare anecdote/praise/emotion at zero.
Both score identification of specific populations/firms/places/users bearing distinct costs and benefits plus an account of unequal exposure or access.
Both score duplicated wording, headings, demands, or paragraph order indicating form-campaign text versus original individualized wording.
Both score abundance of portal/email headers, attachment placeholders, filenames, OCR errors, duplicated cover text, and page artifacts as a surface feature.
Both require an exact identified provision plus a concrete revision to it, with bare support or opposition at zero.
Both score prominence of advertised organizational size, market share, longevity, assets, employees, facilities, or senior titles.
Both score only the letter furniture (formal salutation plus signature block); the explicit intermediate-score note makes the same scale explicit rather than changing it.
Both score precise mapping of the proposal onto docket provisions, CFR sections, statutory authority, or requested edits, versus broad support/opposition.
Both score supply of exact replacement language, thresholds, definitions, procedures, or parameters, with 'do more/act quickly'/bare position at zero.
Both score attention to actors, workflows, training, system dependencies, and failure modes that determine practical workability, versus treating implementation as automatic.

Citing CFR parts and sections is a surface citation feature, while arguing the statute does not authorize the rule is a developed substantive legal claim; a comment can easily have one without the other.
Both score whether a specific actionable gap in the proposal is located and what filling it would require, with identical 10/5/0 anchors in prose versus numbered form.
Both score the bare presence of any digit-bearing quantity anywhere in the text, explicitly ignoring its use or correctness.
Intensity of expressed feeling and description of one's own operational practice are distinct properties; an outraged comment with no practice detail scores high on one and zero on the other.
Both score a specific in-power procedural request with a record-grounded reason, using the same examples and the same 10/5/0 structure.
Both require a quoted or cited term, at least two readings, and their divergent consequences, with 'unclear' assertions at 5 and no textual engagement at 0.
Both score distinguishing strong from weak evidence, naming assumptions or limitations, and calibrating confidence, versus treating all claims as certain.
Both score whether a step-by-step causal chain (including behavioral response where relevant) links the rule to the claimed effect; the added partial-credit note only makes the middle explicit.
